19:4.text: And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

provenance.other: "many mighty works" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Matthew 13:58. The bare phrase 'mighty works' is common in the Synoptics; the quantified form is not, and Matthew 13:58 is the only place the KJV counts them.
provenance.significance: Matthew 13:58 is the KJV's one sentence about mighty works *not* done, and the reason it gives is unbelief — Jesus in his own country, among people who know his family. Alma 19 opens by putting that sentence into the mouth of a Lamanite queen about a Nephite stranger, and two verses later the narrator explains what has happened to her husband in exactly the countervailing term: 'the dark veil of unbelief being cast away from his mind' (19:6). The one KJV verse in which unbelief stops the works is thus the verse the chapter answers, and it is answered in a foreign court rather than a home town. Matthew's Nazareth asks 'is not this the carpenter's son?'; Lamoni's servants have asked whether Ammon is the Great Spirit or a man (18:3), and the queen has settled it as 'a prophet of a Holy God.'

19:4.note: 'That thou art a prophet of a Holy God, and that thou hast power to do many mighty works in his name.' A three-word KJV singleton, and the only quantified 'mighty works' in the Bible. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; catalogued as an allusion on the rarity and on the direct contact with the chapter's own vocabulary of unbelief at 19:6. The queen's clause is the affirmative of Matthew's negative: where Matthew reports mighty works withheld for unbelief, she reports power to do them and asks for one.

19:5.text: Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.

provenance.other: "he stinketh" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 11:39. "two days and two nights" occurs in none — the KJV's countable interval before a raising is John's four days and the Synoptics' three days and three nights.
provenance.significance: This is where the chapter names its source, and it names it by contradiction. In John 11 the woman closest to the dead man is the one who raises the objection: the stone should stay, the body has turned, four days have passed. In Alma 19 the queen reports the objection as other people's — 'some say that he is not dead, but others say that he is dead, and that he stinketh' — and then refuses it in her own person: 'but as for myself, to me he doth not stink.' Martha's sentence is thus split in two and the queen is given the better half. The metalepsis is worth stating plainly: John's raising narrative is the one in which decay is admitted and overruled, and the Book of Mormon has taken the admission, put it in the crowd's mouth, and made the woman's private judgment the ground of the faith Ammon commends five verses later.

19:5.note: 'And that he stinketh, and that he ought to be placed in the sepulchre; but as for myself, to me he doth not stink.' A KJV singleton in the KJV's one four-day raising, and the verse that identifies which raising narrative this chapter is running. The 19:1 burial preparation, the sepulchre 'which they had made for the purpose of burying their dead', and the interval counted in days are all in place before the phrase arrives. What follows in the chapter confirms it: 'not dead, but sleepeth' at 19:8 (John 11:11) and 'Believest thou this?' at 19:9 (John 11:26, another singleton). The three occur in John's order.

19:8.text: And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth.

provenance.route: Mark 5:39 and John 11:11-23 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: "not dead, but sleepeth" occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Matthew 9:24, Mark 5:39, Luke 8:52 — all three of Jairus's daughter. Only Mark and Luke add the entry into the house that Alma 19:7 has just narrated ('he went in to see the king'); Mark alone has 'when he was come in, he saith'. 'Shall rise again' occurs in 5 verses, of which John 11:23, 'Thy brother shall rise again', is the only one not about the third day of Christ's own passion.
provenance.significance: Two raisings are fused in a single sentence, and each supplies what the other lacks. From Jairus's daughter comes the diagnosis — the body is asleep, the mourners are wrong, and the physician says so on entering the house. From Lazarus comes the promise with a date on it: 'Thy brother shall rise again', which Martha at once postpones to the last day and Jesus at once brings forward. Ammon does the bringing forward himself — 'on the morrow he shall rise again' — and so removes the misunderstanding that John 11:24 is built on. The result is a raising narrative in which nobody is wrong except the crowd, and it is followed by the one instruction Jesus never has to give at either tomb: 'therefore bury him not.'

19:8.note: 'He is not dead, but he sleepeth in God, and on the morrow he shall rise again; therefore bury him not.' The four-word run belongs to one Gospel episode in three tellings, and 'shall rise again' pulls the other. 'He sleepeth in God' is not KJV and is the sentence's one theological addition — the Book of Mormon has already told the reader at 19:6 what the sleep is, a mind overcome by the light of the glory of God, which is neither Mark's death nor John's.

19:9.text: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?

provenance.other: "Believest thou this" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 11:26. The answer follows John 11:27's shape as well: 'She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe' becomes 'And she said unto him … nevertheless, I believe.' John 11:27 is already a source in this book, adjudicated at Alma 6:8 for 'the Son of God which should come'.
provenance.significance: The chapter has been running John 11 since 19:5, and here it takes the question the whole chapter of John turns on — the one Jesus puts to Martha before the tomb, on which the raising is conditioned. What the Book of Mormon changes is the ground of the answer. Martha answers a confession: 'I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God.' The queen answers an evidentiary complaint and then believes anyway — 'I have had no witness, save thy word, and the word of our servants; nevertheless, I believe.' Belief on testimony alone rather than on sight is John's own closing beatitude at 20:29, and it is what makes Ammon's next sentence possible: a woman outside the covenant people is told her faith exceeds anything inside it. Martha is never told that. She is inside.

19:9.note: 'And Ammon saith unto her, Believest thou this? And she said unto him, I have had no witness, save thy word … nevertheless, I believe.' Three words, and a KJV singleton, arriving fourth in a run of John 11 contacts (11:39 at 19:5; 11:11 and 11:23 at 19:8; 11:26-27 here) that occur in John's order. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the singleton and the sequence rather than the length — far below Skousen's threshold and not one of his thirty-six. Alma 15:6 has already staged a healing as a catechism on Matthew 9:28's 'Believe ye that I am able to do this?'; this is the same operation on a different singleton, and the two together are becoming a habit of the book's missionary narratives. The 1830 'saith' for the narrative past, regularized to 'said' in 1920, survives in Ammon's half of the exchange and not the queen's, which is the KJV's own asymmetry in John 11:26-27.

19:10.text: When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

provenance.other: "so great faith" occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Matthew 8:10 and Luke 7:9, in identical words — the same centurion in two Gospels. Nothing in Alma 19:10 discriminates between them, and the row is filed at Matthew 8:10 with Luke 7:9 named here rather than silently dropped. "O woman" and "great is thy faith" are each KJV singletons at Matthew 15:28, and 'speak the word only' is a singleton at Matthew 8:8.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly two people whose faith is praised as exceeding Israel's, and both are Gentiles who ask for a household member to be healed at a distance: the centurion, and the woman of Canaan. Alma 19:9-10 is built out of both. From the centurion comes the structure — belief on the bare word ('I have had no witness, save thy word'; compare 'speak the word only'), and then the pronouncement measured against the covenant people, with 'the Nephites' standing where the KJV has 'Israel'. From the Canaanite woman comes the address: Ammon breaks his sentence to say 'I say unto thee, woman', which is Matthew 15:28's vocative and is not otherwise how this book speaks to anyone. What the substitution does is precise. 'No, not in Israel' is a rebuke of Israel; 'among all the people of the Nephites' is a rebuke of the Nephites, delivered by a Nephite in a Lamanite palace, in a chapter that ends with a Lamanite church.

19:10.note: 'Blessed art thou, because of thy exceeding faith; I say unto thee, woman, there has not been such great faith among all the people of the Nephites.' Two Gospel pericopes fused, and the fusion is legible because each contributes something the other has not: the comparative measure of faith against the covenant nation (Matthew 8:10 / Luke 7:9) and the vocative 'woman' with the praise of her faith (Matthew 15:28). 'Blessed art thou' is common in the KJV (5 verses) and carries no weight on its own; the row rests on the two-verse phrase and the singleton vocative.

19:12.text: Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his:

provenance.other: "Blessed be the name of God" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Daniel 2:20. The far commoner formula is 'blessed be the name of the LORD' (Job 1:21, Psalm 113:2, and others); the substitution of 'God' for 'the LORD' is Daniel's alone.
provenance.significance: Alma 18 built the court scene out of Daniel — Belshazzar's changed countenance at Daniel 5:6, the offer of anything at 5:16, the thoughts of the heart at 2:30 — and this is the frame closing. Daniel 2:20 is the doxology Daniel speaks the moment the king's secret is revealed to him, before he goes in to the king; Alma 19:12 is the doxology the king himself speaks the moment he wakes. The Book of Mormon has moved the blessing from the interpreter to the interpreted, which is what the whole Ammon narrative is doing to the Daniel pattern: in Daniel the foreign king is never converted, he only acknowledges; here he rises, blesses God, and preaches (19:31).

19:12.note: 'And as he arose, he stretched forth his hand unto the woman, and said, Blessed be the name of God, and blessed art thou.' A six-word KJV singleton in the mouth of the risen king. 'Stretched forth his hand' is 7 KJV verses and carries nothing; the row is the doxology. Note where it stands in the chapter's economy — Lamoni's first act on waking is to bless God and then his wife, which is the inversion of 19:5, where the wife's private judgment against the crowd was all that stood between him and a sepulchre.

19:13.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:

provenance.other: "redeemer liveth" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Job 19:25, and 'my redeemer' in only 2 (Job 19:25 and Psalm 19:14). "born of a woman" occurs in 3, all of them Job — 14:1, 15:14, 25:4 — and in every one it means frail, short-lived and unclean; the KJV never uses it of Christ, whose incarnation at Galatians 4:4 is 'made of a woman'.
provenance.significance: Lamoni's confession is Job 19:25 with the verb moved. Job says 'I know that my redeemer liveth'; Lamoni says 'as sure as thou livest, behold, I have seen my Redeemer' — the living is transferred to the woman he is addressing, and what is predicated of the Redeemer is instead sight, which is Job's next verse and not his twenty-fifth ('yet in my flesh shall I see God … mine eyes shall behold'). The chapter has earned the transfer: Job speaks his confession out of a body eaten by worms, and Lamoni speaks his out of a body the court has just declared to stink. And the phrase the Book of Mormon then attaches to the Redeemer — 'born of a woman' — is the phrase Job uses three times for everything that makes a man perishable. Applied to the one who will 'redeem all mankind', it says that the Redeemer takes on precisely the condition Job's formula names.

19:13.note: 'For as sure as thou livest, behold, I have seen my Redeemer; and he shall come forth, and be born of a woman.' The verbal contact is distributed rather than continuous — 'liveth', 'my Redeemer', 'seen', 'born of a woman' — which is why the n-gram stream proposed nothing at this verse; a contiguous window cannot see it (CONVENTIONS §9). Two of the four elements are KJV singletons or near it, and all four come from one passage of Job apart from the shared 'born of a woman' formula, which is Job's as well. Recorded at 'high' rather than 'certain' because none of the four is a reproduced clause.

19:17.text: And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy.

provenance.other: "her mistress" occurs in 5 KJV verses; the collocation 'said unto her mistress' in exactly 1, 2 Kings 5:3. Alma 19:17 has 'her mistress, the queen', which is the Book of Mormon's only use of the word.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one servant woman who knows something about the true God that her foreign master's household does not, and whose telling of it sets the household's healing in motion: the little maid taken captive out of Israel who waits on Naaman's wife. She has no name, she speaks once, and the whole of 2 Kings 5 follows from her sentence. Abish is her counterpart with the terms reversed — a Lamanite, not an Israelite; converted in her own country by a vision of her father's, not carried off; silent for years rather than speaking once ('thus having been converted to the Lord, never had made it known'). And the outcome is reversed too. Naaman's healing converts one man who then asks for two mules' burden of earth to worship on; Abish's telling produces a church (19:35). Luke 4:27 makes Naaman the standing type of the outsider healed while Israel is passed over, which is the same argument Ammon has just made at 19:10 in the centurion's words — two independent KJV texts saying that faith outside the covenant people has outrun faith inside it, and the chapter uses both.

19:17.note: 'And also her mistress, the queen … therefore she ran forth from house to house, making it known unto the people.' Catalogued as figural: the verbal contact is 'her mistress' and the shape of the scene, not a run of words. It is written because the KJV's servant-woman-who-knows type has exactly one instance, because Alma 19 uses the one word that instance uses, and because the narrator goes out of his way at 19:16-17 to establish precisely the two facts 2 Kings 5:2-3 establishes about the maid — that she serves in the household and that she has knowledge of God the household lacks.
19:17.whyNot: A named servant with a private faith is a stock figure and needs no source, and 'her mistress' is the ordinary English for the relation. A reader may hold that Abish's function in the plot — to fetch a crowd — is generated by the narrative's own needs and that the resemblance to 2 Kings 5 is a resemblance between two stories that both require a servant to start them.

19:24.text: And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.

provenance.other: "fear came upon" occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Job 4:14, Acts 2:43 and Acts 5:11 — and only the Acts pair follows a sudden death in an apostle's presence. 'Durst' occurs in 4 verses, of which Acts 5:13 is the one that describes a crowd afraid to approach. Acts 5 is already an established source in this book: the lie to the Holy Ghost stands behind Alma 10:25, 11:25 and 12:3.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:1-13 is the New Testament's one sequence in which a man drops dead in front of an apostle, fear falls on everyone who hears of it, and the people afterwards will not come near — 'of the rest durst no man join himself to them.' Alma 19:22-24 runs the same three beats: the Lamanite lifts his sword at Ammon and falls dead, 'fear came upon them all', and 'they durst not put forth their hands to touch him'. The moral direction is inverted, which is the interesting part. In Acts the dead are the liars inside the church and the fear disciplines the believers; here the dead man is an assailant from outside and the fear protects the missionary. Both texts then draw the same conclusion — that the untouchability is a fact about power and not about the man — and Alma 19:23 says so outright, in the language of an oath given to Mosiah rather than of a judgment: 'I will spare him, and it shall be unto him according to thy faith.'

19:24.note: 'Fear came upon them all, and they durst not put forth their hands to touch him.' Two of the three KJV verses with 'fear came upon' are in Acts, and the nearer of them stands eight verses from the only KJV crowd that 'durst' not approach a wonder-working preacher. Held at moderate: neither phrase is a singleton, and the sequence rather than any one string is the evidence. Note that 'put forth their hands' is a KJV singleton at Psalm 125:3, where it means to reach after iniquity — an unrelated sense, and not the source.
19:24.whyNot: The two contacts are three-verse and four-verse phrases, not singletons, and a crowd frightened by a sudden death is the natural thing for a narrator to write without a model. The row would be withdrawn if the Acts 5 language elsewhere in Alma turned out to be the book's own formula rather than a borrowing.

19:29.text: And he gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive.

provenance.other: "gave her his hand" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 9:41, and "by the hand, and lifted her up" in exactly 1, Mark 1:31. "took her by the hand" occurs in 3 verses (Matthew 9:25, Mark 1:31, Luke 8:54), all of raising or curing a woman. "stood upon her feet" occurs in none. Mark 1:31 has already been adjudicated in this book at Alma 15:6, for the hand-taking that cures Zeezrom's fever.
provenance.significance: In the KJV, raising a prostrate woman by the hand belongs to Christ and to Peter, and in Acts 9 it is done to Tabitha in a room full of widows, after which 'it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord.' Alma 19 gives the gesture to a woman — Abish takes the queen by the hand, and the queen then takes the king by the hand at 19:30, so the raising passes down a chain of three with no apostle in it at all. The Book of Mormon is careful about what this does and does not claim: 'that perhaps she might raise her from the ground' concedes that Abish does not know whether it will work, and the verse credits the rising to the touch rather than to a word of power. What follows is Tabitha's Joppa — knowledge spreading through the city, and many believing (19:31-35).

19:29.note: 'She went and took the queen by the hand, that perhaps she might raise her from the ground; and as soon as she touched her hand, she arose and stood upon her feet.' Catalogued at moderate. Taking a fallen person's hand needs no source, and the phrase the Book of Mormon uses is not exactly any of the three KJV forms; what carries the row is that the KJV's hand-raisings of women are a small and coherent set, that Alma 19:29-30 performs two of them in succession, and that the aftermath follows Acts 9:42. The 'perhaps' is not in any of them and is worth noticing — the one uncertain hand in the group is the one that belongs to a servant.
19:29.whyNot: No run of KJV wording is reproduced. A reader may take the gesture as the obvious way to get a fallen queen off the ground and decline the whole set.

19:30.text: For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries.

provenance.other: "no man understandeth" is a KJV singleton at 1 Corinthians 14:2. The Book of Mormon's 'speaking many words which were not understood' has the same predicate in the passive and no other shared word.
provenance.significance: Paul's chapter is the Bible's one sustained account of speech that nobody present can construe, and its whole argument is that such speech edifies no one until it is interpreted. Alma 19:30 gives the queen exactly that speech at exactly the moment the crowd outside is in contention over what has happened — and the narrative agrees with Paul: her unintelligible words change nothing, and what ends the contention is Lamoni's plain preaching in the next verse of 'the words which he had heard from the mouth of Ammon.' The chapter has already glossed one foreign word in the KJV's own formula at 18:13; here it declines to gloss, and the declining is the point.

19:30.note: 'She clasped her hands, being filled with joy, speaking many words which were not understood.' A single shared idea and one singleton predicate, so this is filed as an echo and not more. It is written because the Book of Mormon rarely reports unintelligible speech and because the sequence of 19:29-31 reproduces Paul's argument about it — ecstatic utterance, no effect, then intelligible preaching and conversion — without using Paul's vocabulary of tongues at all.
19:30.whyNot: The contact is one word, in a different voice, and a narrator describing joy that overflows language would write this sentence with no source in front of him. There is no 'tongue' or 'interpret' anywhere in the chapter to confirm that 1 Corinthians 14 is in view.

19:36.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: "believe on his name" occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, John 1:12; so does the shorter 'on his name'. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice in this chapter, at 19:13 and again in the closing sentence here, and it has entered the book earlier at Alma 11:40.
provenance.significance: John 1:12 is the prologue's definition of who is admitted — not those born of blood or of the will of man, but as many as receive him — and the Book of Mormon puts its singleton at the end of the chapter in which a Lamanite court becomes a church. 'His arm is extended to all people who will repent and believe on his name' answers the prologue's next clause about birth and lineage with the argument this whole chapter has been making by narrative: the Lamanite queen's faith exceeded any among the Nephites (19:10), and the terms of admission are therefore not national.

19:36.note: 'We see that his arm is extended to all people who will repent and believe on his name.' A four-word KJV singleton closing the chapter. Frederick's monograph is an argument about the Gospel of John in the Book of Mormon and his discussion of John 1:12 falls in the same passage of his book as this verse; the catalogue's index of him records that co-occurrence and nothing stronger, and no claim about what he identifies is made here. The 'arm extended' half of the sentence is the book's own formula and is not Isaiah 5:25's 'his hand is stretched out still', which carries the opposite sense.
